title: EUR 7.5 billion Just Transition Fund too small for its scope
problem: Coal and carbon-intensive regions face heavy job losses, with IRENA estimating up to 1.6 million energy-sector jobs at risk in 2021–2027.
solution: The Commission proposed a Just Transition Fund of EUR 7.5 billion in new EU money, topped up by transfers from ERDF and ESF+ envelopes and national co-financing, covering social support, economic revitalisation and land restoration in regions with approved territorial plans.
funding: EU budget (2021–2027 MFF), with EUR 1.5 to 3 of ERDF/ESF+ transfers per EUR 1 of JTF money plus national co-financing.
results: Bruegel found no justification for the EUR 7.5 billion figure; its rough lower-bound estimate for retraining energy-sector workers alone is about EUR 10.8 billion, so it suggests refocusing the fund on social support and retraining.
serbia_reason: On accession Serbia's lignite regions would enter this EU funding model, and the analysis shows EU transition grants cover only part of the need. Serbian planners should not expect EU grants alone to pay for the transition.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to combine pre-accession funds with national budget and development-bank finance, and target grants at worker support.
blockers: Serbia cannot access the Just Transition Fund before EU accession.
quote: This totals roughly EUR10.8 billion, which is already above the JTF’s proposed allocation of EUR 7.5 billion.

title: Territorial transition plans lack binding fossil fuel phase-out dates
programme: Territorial Just Transition Plans (Just Transition Fund proposal)
problem: Transition support needs clear long-term phase-out timelines so workers, investors and regions can plan.
solution: To access the fund, countries must submit territorial plans, approved by the Commission, setting out a timeline of transition steps, the most affected territories (down to NUTS3), their challenges, governance arrangements and consistency with national energy and climate plans.
funding: Access to Just Transition Fund grants depends on plan approval.
results: Interviewed stakeholders valued the fine-grained targeting but found the plans resource- and time-intensive, a hurdle for low-capacity countries; Bruegel notes the plans do not require clear phase-out goals and suggests rewarding ambitious plans in the allocation formula.
serbia_reason: Serbia's energy and climate plan and any future transition plans for Kolubara and Kostolac will be judged against EU requirements like these. Adding a firm lignite exit date would make them stronger than the EU minimum.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need regional administrative capacity to prepare plans at this level of detail.
blockers: Limited administrative capacity in Serbian municipalities and the absence of a national coal exit date.
quote: However, it should be noted that these Plans do not require Member States to give clear and long-term fossil fuel phase-out goals, which could hinder efforts to plan for the transition.

title: EU coal regions platform valued but weak on inclusion and transparency
programme: Platform for Coal Regions in Transition
problem: Coal regions needed a way to share practice, project ideas and funding information for their transition.
solution: Since 2017 the Commission has run a voluntary platform for public authorities, NGOs, unions, industry, citizen groups and academia, with technical support from the Commission and the EIB's JASPERS and a secretariat added in early 2019.
delivery_partners: Secretariat run by Ecorys, ICLEI, Climate Strategies Europe and the Wuppertal Institute
results: After 6 working group meetings and two annual political dialogues, all interviewed stakeholders welcomed it for knowledge sharing and networking; but country meetings lacked transparency, NGOs and unions took part only ad hoc, and a Romanian respondent said it was not truly owned by the government.
serbia_reason: A Western Balkans version of such a platform is the most direct EU support channel for Serbia's coal regions. The weaknesses found here show what to insist on: open country meetings and structured roles for unions and NGOs.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to open its country-level meetings to non-government stakeholders and tie platform work to national decisions.
blockers: Weak government ownership, as reported for Romania, could leave the platform as talk without projects.
quote: More generally, some participants felt there was not enough of a structured way to involve all stakeholders, and NGOs, trade unions and citizen groups were only involved on an ad hoc basis.

title: Romania's state-funded coal mine closures failed to re-employ miners
programme: Romanian coal mine closures (Jiu Valley, Oltenia, Prahova)
problem: Uneconomic coal mines run by state-owned companies in the Jiu Valley, Oltenia and Prahova basins had to close, hitting mono-industrial regions.
solution: Since 1997 the state budget, through the line ministry, has financed closures of the state-owned mining companies, with redundancy compensation, training programmes and other social protection for laid-off workers.
funding: Romanian state budget; current closures follow the EU decision on aid for closing uncompetitive hard-coal mines.
results: Since 1989 Jiu Valley mining jobs fell from 54,000 to 3,000, and reintegration of laid-off workers failed because no new economic activities emerged; 5 mines are still being closed under the EU decision on uncompetitive hard-coal mines.
serbia_reason: Serbia's lignite mines belong to the state-owned utility, so closures would also be state-financed and subject to state aid rules. Romania shows that compensation and training alone do not stop long-term decline without new jobs.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to pair closure compensation with an economic diversification plan for Kolubara and Kostolac before mines close.
blockers: Mono-industrial local economies and low capacity to absorb EU funds could repeat Romania's outcome.
quote: The mine closure measures included the right to compensation for salary following collective redundancy, training programmes and other social protection measures for the former employees. Even so, the reintegration of the laid-off personnel was unsuccessful because of the failure to create new economic activities able to absorb the available work force.

title: Greece's rapid lignite exit lacks territorial plans and social dialogue
programme: Greek lignite phase-out (existing plants retired by 2023)
problem: Western Macedonia and Megalopolis depend heavily on lignite; Western Macedonia had 27% unemployment in 2018.
solution: The Greek government decided to retire all existing lignite plants by 2023, leaving one unit under construction to run between 2023 and 2028.
funding: No steady public financing was in place, and Greece's share of the proposed Just Transition Mechanism was judged limited.
results: Months before the first plant, Amyntaio, was due to close there were no coherent territorial plans, no social partner dialogue and no consultation; about 7,175 people still worked in the lignite industry at the end of 2019.
serbia_reason: Like Greece's PPC, Serbia's state-owned utility runs lignite plants that anchor regional economies. Greece shows that a fast top-down exit decision without regional plans leaves communities unprepared.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need a just transition committee of ministries, municipalities, unions, NGOs and the utility, with an agreed master plan before closures start.
blockers: Plant economics or EU rules could force closures before transition plans and funding are ready.
quote: This is exacerbated by the lack of coherent territorial plans for the two regions or a robust governance structure, just a few months before the shut-down of the first lignite plant in Amyntaio. To further worsen the situation, there currently exists no dialogue between the social partners influenced by the phase out decision and no consultation process for the development of the territorial transition plans.

title: Silesia redirects EU regional funds to coal-region transformation projects
programme: Action Plan for Transformation of Silesia (Silesian regional operational programme)
problem: Silesia, the EU's largest mining region with about 75.5 thousand mining jobs, faces mine closures, depopulation and severe air pollution.
solution: The regional government joined the EU coal regions platform as a pilot region, adopted an Action Plan for Transformation in July 2019 and redirected part of its EU-funded regional operational programme to transformation projects.
implementer: Marshal Office of the Silesian Voivodeship
funding: EU cohesion funds through the EUR 3.5 billion Silesian regional operational programme.
results: The region redirected EUR 120 million to transformation projects and leads 14 regional pilot projects, while 14 unprofitable mining operations are being liquidated with Commission-approved public aid; the national government had no official plans for further mine closures.
serbia_reason: Shows a coal region using EU funds and EU-approved state aid for mine closures to start its own transition. Serbia's mining regions could channel EU pre-accession funds the same way, within state aid rules.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need regional bodies with the capacity to manage EU-funded programmes, which Silesia built over 13 years.
blockers: Serbia's centralised fund management and lack of national closure plans could limit regional initiative.
quote: The region redirected 120 million euro of regional operational programme allocation to transformation projects till now.

title: Enel's Futur-e redeploys all workers from closed power plants
problem: Enel needed to close and convert 23 thermoelectric plants and one mining site without leaving workers behind.
solution: From 2015 Enel involved local stakeholders to find new uses for each site, reused existing infrastructure, and retrained and redeployed all employees to other units or locations.
results: As of 2019 all workers from affected sites had been relocated on a voluntary basis, helped by non-conflictual industrial relations and the company's detailed data on workers' skills and needs.
serbia_reason: Serbia's utility could use a similar internal redeployment model for staff at the lignite plants and mines it closes. It shows a utility with good skills data and union relations can avoid layoffs.
adapt_needed: The Serbian utility would need a workforce skills database and new internal roles, for example in renewables, to absorb workers.
blockers: The Serbian utility has fewer new business lines than Enel to absorb redeployed staff.
quote: As of 2019, all workers from affected sites had been relocated on a voluntary basis (Galgóczi, 2019).

title: Ruhr's early support for incumbent coal firms delayed transition
problem: Coal jobs in the Ruhr, where one in ten inhabitants worked in mining in the mid-1950s, were halved by the mid-1960s.
solution: Public policy first propped up the established coal and steel companies into the 1970s; from the 1980s it shifted to start-ups, technology firms, services and universities, backed by early retirement, retraining and mobility policies.
results: Labour policies cushioned much of the shock, but years of lock-in left unemployment and poverty far above the national average, cities in critical financial condition and the Emscher river heavily polluted.
serbia_reason: Serbia risks a similar lock-in if policy keeps propping up lignite mining instead of preparing alternatives. The Ruhr shows that delay makes the eventual transition longer and costlier.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to shift support from sustaining lignite to new firms and skills early, before mines decline.
blockers: A coalition of officials, the utility, unions and communities with a stake in lignite may resist early change.
quote: When faced with these significant losses, public policy was initially aimed at supporting the established coal and steel companies and remained that way well into the 1970s. This resulted from a coalition of policymakers, investors, community leaders and workers who all had a vested interest in maintaining the status quo, which had provided them with stable jobs, strong returns on investments and even a sense of identity, pride and community for decades.
